name: Baba Malay
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification rests on the language's modern reference description (Lee 2014 UH PhD, Glottolog type 'grammar', 473 pp), in a dedicated word-stress section illustrated with Praat pitch/intensity tracks; the quotation is verbatim at the cited pages and Lee's own stress transcriptions (final primary, alternating secondary leftward: ˌke.ro.ˈsi, ter.ˌba.lék.ˈkan, ku.ˌpu.ku.ˈpu) reproduce alternating stress from the right exactly, with her hedge 'tends to' supporting dominant rather than strict. The record showed we have no copy and a blank grade; the deciding PDF is now obtained by the project and confirmed, so the grade can be set (typeset PDF, quote verified). The only better-credentialed item is the same author's 2022 De Gruyter book version (paywalled), unlikely to change the classification; Lim 1988 (downloaded) is silent, and the remaining Glottolog items are older UMI dissertations or an irrelevant mis-linked review (Winkelmann 201

sources.citation: Lee 2014, A Grammar of Baba Malay, UH Manoa PhD, sec 3.6.1 pp.100-106 (full PDF from ScholarSpace bitstream d1f39d65)
sources.quote: Thus, in disyllabic words featuring both open and closed syllables, lexical stress always occurs on the ultimate syllable. ... in trisyllabic BM words, primary stress falls on the ultimate syllable, followed by the first syllable. ... stress allocation begins from the ultimate syllable

sources.citation: Lee, Nala Huiying. 2014. A grammar of Baba Malay with sociophonetic considerations. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. ScholarSpace hdl 10125/101107, bitstream d1f39d65.
sources.quote: 'In BM, pitch is the most accurate indicator of stress. The ultimate syllable tends to receive the most stress. ... when there are three syllables, the final syllable receives the most stress, followed by the first syllable. Lexical stress allocation begins from the final syllable, and stress alternates between syllables. Words with four syllables ... the ultimate syllable receives the most stress, the penultimate syllable is not stressed, and the second syllable is stressed.' (p.100); examples o.ˈrang, pan.ˈjat, ra.ˈsa, ˌke.ro.ˈsi, ˌba.lék.ˈkan, ter.ˌba.lék.ˈkan, ku.ˌpu.ku.ˈpu.
sources.locator: sec. 3.6.1 Word stress and pitch, printed pp.100-106 (pp.119-125)

sources.citation: Lim, Sonny. 1988. Baba Malay: the language of the 'Straits-born' Chinese. In H. Steinhauer (ed.), Papers in Western Austronesian Linguistics No. 3, 1-61. Pacific Linguistics A-78. Canberra: ANU. hdl 1885/145107.
sources.quote: No word-stress statement; only remark is that the function word punya 'receives no stress within the sentence contour'.
sources.locator: pp.1-61; p.2 states the investigation 'is essentially on the syntactic structure of Baba Malay rather than on its phonological structure'
